title: A route through the numbers
bodyMd:
Original public-policy exposition with a table.

A transit office tested a revised bus route for six weeks. The revision bypassed two low-use stops and added a stop beside an evening training center. The office collected average weekday boardings in three time periods before the trial and during its final two weeks. It used the same counting method throughout.

| Time period | Before trial | Final two trial weeks |
|---|---:|---:|
| Morning | 240 | 236 |
| Afternoon | 180 | 184 |
| Evening | 80 | 120 |

The office called the trial encouraging because total boardings rose. At a public meeting, however, a former user of a bypassed stop pointed out that boardings count trips, not individual people. A small number of new riders making frequent journeys could outweigh the loss of several people who previously rode occasionally. The office had not collected information about the number of distinct riders.

A training-center employee offered another caution. A new course had started during the trial, and enrollment would fall when it ended. That did not show the evening gain was temporary, but it did identify a condition the office should test before treating the gain as permanent.

The office extended the trial through the following course break and added an anonymous rider survey. Its revised goal was not merely to determine whether the buses carried more trips, but to understand who benefited and whether the change would last. The initial counts remained useful; they simply could not answer every question raised at the meeting.
